(Subject: Tantra) Oṃ. Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Dattātreya, with palms joined in reverence, questioned Maheśvara, the God of gods, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, as he sat upon the peak of Kailāsa. Being affectionate toward his devotees, he asked for the sake of the welfare of his followers: "The Kalpa-tantra is being narrated; it is a great manual for attaining success in the Kali age."

They describe the ritual application of the Tantric sciences to Maheśvara, the Great God of gods. There exist in this world various types of yantras, mantras, and magical rites (abhicāra)—those spoken in the Āgamas, those spoken in the Purāṇas, those spoken in the Vedas, as well as the Ḍāmara, the Uḍīśa, the Kālacaṇḍeśvara-mata, the Rādhā-tantra, the Ucchiṣṭa, the Dhārā-tantra, and the Mṛteśvara.

Having performed the "pinning" (kīlana) of all those [rites], they become devoid of power in the Kali age; even a Brāhmaṇa who possesses desire and anger acts for that very reason, without the pinning.

"O Śiva, how are the Kama-mantras and the Tantra-vidyās? What is the characteristic of Tantra-vidyā? O Lord, show me the grace that brings about success. The Lord said: "Listen, O accomplished great yogin, expert in all Tantras! The Tantra-vidyā is a great secret, difficult even for the gods to attain. It has been told by my mouth; it is the crest-jewel of the deities' Tantra-vidyās. Secret, secret, secret, a great secret—secret again and again! It should be given to one devoted to the Guru, but never to one who is not a devotee. [It should be given] to one whose mind is solely devoted to Śiva, and not to one of wicked heart..."

One should give one’s head, one should give one’s city, and one should give whatever is required there; it must not be withheld from anyone, for this was spoken by Śaṅkara. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Dattātreyatantra; listen likewise. In the Kali age, this great tantra is said to bring success even without a *kīla* (pinning rite). There is no requirement for a lunar day (*tithi*), nor a constellation (*nakṣatra*), nor a restriction, nor a specific day of the week. It is free from vows, observances, and burnt offerings (*homa*), and devoid of considerations of time or hour. Success in the form of a command (*preṣa*) arises through the mantra alone; by the mere practice of which, in an instant—

And accomplishment arises: killing, deluding, paralyzing, causing hatred, summoning, subjugating, attracting, sorcery, the science of Yakṣiṇīs, elixirs, knowledge of time, freedom from hunger, stealing, the discovery of treasures, the yoga for making a barren woman pregnant, restoring life to one whose children have died, rejuvenation through mere recitation, warding off spirits and planetary afflictions, and likewise [protection against] the fear of lions, tigers, snakes, and scorpions. Curd, milk, honey, and ghee—there is nothing else, as declared by Śaṅkara. This must be kept secret, kept secret, it is great.

To be hidden, hidden, hidden again and again. *Oṃ*, salutations to the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self. Salutations to Dattātreya, who is Brahmā, Hari, and Hara; who causes creation, maintenance, and dissolution; whose nature consists of the three *guṇas*; and who displays all wonders. Grant success in the *tantras*, grant it, *svāhā*. [Thus ends the first chapter in the Śrī-Dattātreya-Īśvara-saṃvāda. Now, regarding the rite of killing (*māraṇa*): The Lord said—If one should cast upon the ground the body of someone [mixed with] funeral ashes, poison, and the powder of a *dhatura* plant, [that person shall die].
Oil extracted from *bhallātaka* mixed with the fang-poison of a black cobra and the juice of *dhattūra*, when applied to someone's body, causes immediate death.

Human bone powder consumed in betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) certainly brings about death. If one throws the powder of a snake’s bones onto someone's body, that person shall meet their end. Furthermore, having taken wood from a funeral pyre on a Tuesday coinciding with the *Bharaṇī* asterism, if one buries it at the door of a house, death will occur within a month. One should take the tail of a black cobra and set it ablaze.

At night, one should prepare collyrium (kajjala) from the oil of a bowstring in a human skull, combined with funeral-ground ashes and five parts of salt; if this powder is applied to someone's body, he will go to the abode of Yama.
Taking the flesh of a scorpion and a thorn, combined with the aforementioned powder, if this powder is applied to someone's body, that man will meet his death.

On the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight, one should draw a yantra and smear it with funeral-ground ashes; if one casts this yantra into the fire of a cremation ground on a Tuesday, the enemy shall die. Having taken the excrement of an owl...

If one casts this powder mixed with *tuviṣa* upon the body of anyone, that person goes immediately to the abode of Yama. Taking the dung of a donkey and mixing it with *tuviṣa* powder, if one casts that powder upon the body of anyone, that person goes immediately to the abode of Yama. Taking the dung of an enemy and holding it in a human skull, if one writes the name of someone while casting it upon the ground in a garden, the enemy shall die as soon as that dung is consumed. This must not be given to just anyone; otherwise, O Śaṅkara, [it will bring misfortune].

If one places *kṛkalāsa* (lizard) fat and oil upon the body of someone who is bowed down by a *vidruma* (coral) [curse], that enemy shall die, even if the Lord himself protects him. If salt mixed with *vijayā* (cannabis) is placed in the house of someone whose name is uttered, his death will truly occur within one month; of this there is no doubt. Now the mantra: *Oṃ namaḥ kālarūpāya amukaṃ bhasmīkuru kuru svāhā*. One should recite it one hundred and eight times for success. Now, regarding the deluding rite (*mohana*), the Lord said: "In the powder of *tulasī*, [mixed with] the juice of *sahadevī*..."

One should grind together realgar (*haratāla*), the eight fragrant substances (*aṣṭagandha*), and the juice of plantain (*kadalī*) to create a *tilaka* that deludes the entire world. When combined with *gorocana*, *vacā*, and *kuṣṭha*, this [mixture] causes even incense, lamps, and clothing to be especially enchanted. Upon merely seeing it, kings, subjects, cattle, and birds are rendered infatuated. Having taken root-betel (*mūlatāmbūla*) and a *tilaka* that deludes the world, along with vermilion (*siṃdūra*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and *gorocana*, mixed with the juice of the *dhātrī* (myrobalan) and sesame...

One should grind realgar (*manaḥśilā*), camphor (*karpūra*), and plantain juice (*kadalī-rasa*). By applying a tilaka with this very mantra, one becomes a deluder of the world. One should grind vermilion (*sindūra*), *vacā*, white [substance], and betel-nut juice (*tāmbūla-rasa*). By applying a tilaka with this very mantra, one becomes a deluder of the world. Having made a tilaka with *bhṛṅgarāja*, *apāmārga*, *lajāla*, and *sahadevikā*, a man shall delude the three worlds. Taking an *udumbara* flower and making it into a wick by the wise, and having ignited it with fresh butter (*navanīta*), one should collect the soot (*kajjala*).

At night, one should collect soot for the eyes; it enchants the entire world. It must not be given to just anyone, as it is difficult even for the gods to obtain. The juice of white *guñjā*, its flower, and the root of *brahmadaṇḍī*—by merely smearing these upon the body, one enchants the entire world. Having taken white *dūrvā* grass and *haritāla* (yellow orpiment), one should grind them together. By making a *tilaka* (forehead mark) with these, a man enchants the three worlds. Taking the root of white *arka* and combining it with white sandalwood, by making a *tilaka* on the forehead with this, one enchants the entire world. [Having taken...]

One should cause *tulasī* leaves to dry in the shade, combined with the eight fragrant substances (*aṣṭagandha*) and the seeds of *vijayā*. With half a *kapilā* cow’s milk, one should prepare pills (*vaṭaka*) the size of a *ṭaṅka*. When consumed upon rising in the morning, it deludes the entire world. Oil from the seeds of bitter gourd (*kaṭutuṃbī*) should be used to produce a wick like cloth; by applying the soot (*kajjala*) as collyrium to the eyes, one certainly becomes a deluder. Now the mantra: *Oṃ brahma paramātmane namaḥ, delude all people, delude them, svāhā.* (Recite 108 times. [Thus ends the section from Śrī Dattātreya...]

[In this Tantra, the third chapter named "The Deluding" (Mohana). 3. The Lord said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme suppression of fire (*agni-stambhana*). By taking the fat of a frog and mixing it with the juice of *kaumārī*, the mere act of smearing it upon the body results in the suppression of fire. Having taken the milky sap of the *arka* plant and grinding it with the juice of *kaumārī*, the mere act of smearing it upon the body results in the suppression of fire. Taking the juice of the *kadalī* plant and grinding it with the juice of *kumārī*, the mere act of smearing it upon the body results in the suppression of fire.

When combined with *karpūra* (camphor) and applied as an ointment to the bodies of frogs, a paralysis of fire (*agnistambha*) is produced. Taking the root of *kaumārī* together with the root of *kadalī* (plantain), when applied as an ointment to the bodies [of others], a paralysis of fire is produced. Having repeatedly chewed *kaṇā* (long pepper), *marica* (black pepper), and *śuṇṭhī* (ginger), and then eating glowing charcoal, a man’s mouth is never burned. When the body is smeared with the powder of *kaumārī*, it is not burned. Having drunk clarified butter mixed with sugar, one becomes like half-moon Nāga.

Likewise, after licking heated iron, one's face is never burned anywhere; this is the yoga for the immobilization of fire, as declared by Karu, and it is not otherwise. Now the mantra: *Oṃ namo agnirūpāya mama śarīre stambhanaṃ kuru svāhā*. One should recite this one hundred and eight times; then success (*siddhi*) follows. Next is the immobilization of a seat: one should take the impure pits of a leather-worker, as well as dust mixed with the blood of a Caṇḍāla, and cast it upon the body of whomever one desires; in that person's place, immobilization occurs through the joy of this successful yoga.

This must not be given to anyone else; otherwise, it is as Śaṅkara has declared. Having placed white *guñjā* seeds along with earth into a human skull and offered an oblation (*bali*) of milk, there will be rain for that [person]. One should take a branch or creeper from whatever limb one intends to cast [the mixture]; in that person's place, paralysis (*stambha*) shall occur—this is proclaimed as the *Siddhi-yoga*.
Taking the fire from a cremation ground and salt, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*); in whose name this is done, for him there shall be paralysis—this is proclaimed as the *Siddhi-yoga*.
Now the mantra: Oṃ namo digaṃbarāya amuka-āsana-stambhaṃ kuru kuru svāhā. One should recite it one hundred and eight times; the accomplishment is the paralyzing of the intellect.

Having taken *ukṣūviṣṭā* that has been dried in the shade, one should apply it to the betel leaf; this is the supreme method for paralyzing the intellect of enemies. By making a *tilaka* with white mustard (*siddhārtha*) mixed with clay and horse-dung, it becomes the supreme paralysis of the intellect. One should apply a *tilaka* made from *sahadevī*, *apāmārga*, and iron; this causes the paralysis of the intellect of all beings. Now the mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate śatrūṇāṃ buddhistambhanaṃ kuru svāhā*. Now, the paralysis of weapons...

Having ground *viṣṇukrāntā* and *mūlaka* with the juice of *puṣpārka*, if these are worn on the mouth and the head, there shall be no fear of weapons for men; nor shall there be fear of fire, kings, thieves, or enemies. The root of *jātī* thrown quickly into oil is an excellent means for paralyzing weapons. Having tied the root of *darśanā* on the hand, one paralyzes weapons. With a *ketakī* flower on the eyes and the root of *tāḍa* placed in the mouth, and the *kharjūra* plant on the feet and in the hand, the paralysis of the sword is produced. The three red roots, when powdered and mixed with ghee...

One should drink [this] for a day and night; thereafter, one is not harmed by weapons for as long as one lives. One should collect *āpātā*, *śaika*, *śaṅkha*, and *samūha* together. Having taken the root of *apāmārga* under a flower asterism, its mere application as an ointment to the bodies of those [wounded] wards off all weapons. Even the thorny fruit of the date palm (*kharjūra-mukha*), having tied it at the waist, and the *ketakī* placed upon the staff-like arms, along with *arka*, ward off all weapons. Having extracted the root from white *guñjā* under a flower asterism, one should wear it; there is no fear of the sword in one's hand.
On a Sunday during the month of Ārdrā, one should take *vilva* leaves and grind them with tender [substances] equal to poison; this is an ointment for paralyzing weapons. Now the mantra:
"O great Rākṣasa Kumbhakarṇa, born from the womb of the ocean of the Nairṛtas, the Great Blessed One Rudra, who paralyzes the enemy armies, commands!

Svāhā! One should recite this one hundred and eight times for success. Now, regarding the ointment for weapons: one should cause the seeds of *viṣṇukrāntā* to be taken with the power of the mantra; that oil should be taken...
One should prepare pills by combining Haye-yantra, poison, and roots with oil. A person should apply this as a paste to weapons in the measure of eight *kaṅkas*.

When fierce weapons are used in battle, they will be shattered into pieces. Seeing these weapons, cowards will flee from the fight. For a year, no fear of weapons shall exist anywhere. Now the mantra: *Oṃ namo vikarālarūpāya madvābala-parākramāya amukasya bhujabala-bandha* (Salutation to the one of terrifying form, possessed of my strength and prowess; [bind] the arm-strength of such-and-such).
*Yadṛṣṭistambha-parāṅgānidhūna-parapātana-paramahī-tale-haṭ-svāhā*. One should recite this one hundred and eight times for success. Now, the method for paralyzing an army:

having taken the mantra and the *śvetaguñjā* plant according to the ritual procedure, one should cause it to be placed upon a mound or in a cremation ground using black beans (*māṣa*). One should worship the eight Yoginīs:
Aindrī, Māheśvarī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Vaiṣṇavī, Kumārikā, Lakṣmī, and Brahmī, as well as Gaṇapati and Vaṭuka.

Having likewise worshipped the Kṣetrapāla, the immobilization of the enemy army will occur. Having offered separate oblations (*bali*) for each of the ten [directions] according to the ritual procedure—using meat, liquor, flowers, incense, lamps, and food—one must not give it to anyone else; thus has Śaṅkara declared. Now, the mantra: *Oṃ namaḥ kālarātri-śūladhāriṇī mama śatrusainyaṃ staṃbhanaṃ kuru svāhā*. One should recite this one hundred and eight times for success. Now, regarding the protection of the army: having caught a crow on a Tuesday...

One should go toward the commander of the army with the wings of a crow and an owl; otherwise, it is not so, as declared by Śaṅkara. On a Saturday, having taken [these], one should write the mantra together with the person's name upon a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*) using *gorocana* pigment on the wings of a crow and an owl. One should go toward the commander of the army; otherwise, it is not so, as declared by Śaṅkara. At the mere sound [of this], the army will certainly flee into the midst of the ranks. Even at night, elephants and other [animals] will [flee]; otherwise, it is not so, as declared by Śaṅkara. Oṃ, salutation to the one who causes fear, the wielder of the sword; cause my enemy's army to flee, cause them to flee, svāhā! One should recite this one hundred and eight times for success. Having smeared a clay vessel with cremation-ground ashes, one should place it inside a corpse and bind it with a blue thread, including the name of the enemy. When it is cast into a pit of ghee and placed upon a stone, it effects the immobilization of the army; this is declared to be the Siddhi-yoga. Now follows the immobilization of cows, buffaloes, and so forth: having taken the hair of a camel, [one should place it] around the animal...

One should cast [the mantra] into the midst of animals; this is declared to be the yoga for paralyzing them. Now, the paralysis of humans: having taken a cloth from a menstruating woman and combined it with *gorocana*, one should write the name of the person upon a jar; this immediately causes paralysis. Now, the paralysis of clouds: having taken two bricks and placed them in a casket of charnel-ground ashes, one should set them in the middle of a forest;
this is the paralysis of clouds as spoken by the wise Mūladeva. Now, the paralysis of boats: under the asterism of Bharaṇī, one should take milky wood and a five-limbed stake.

One should cast [this] into the boat; this is the "mooring of the boat" (*nauka-stambhana*) spoken by Him who is Mūladeva. Now, for the suppression of sleep (*nidrā-stambhana*): one should employ the root of *hasā*, *madhuka*, and *piṇu*. This will bring about the suppression of sleep. Now, for the suppression of water (*jala-stambhana*): one should prepare a fine powder of the substance called *padmaka* and cast it into a pond, well, lake, or similar body of water; the water will be bound. Now the mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya jala-stambhaya stambhaya naḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*. (108) Now, for the suppression of the womb (*garbha-stambhana*).

If one eats *dhattūra* root mixed with *airaṇḍa* seeds and *vīja*, it acts as a supreme means for arresting conception. By tying *dhattūra* root at the waist, one arrests conception; by tying *siddhārtha* (white mustard) root on the head, a woman who has given birth will not conceive again. The powder of *dhattūra* root placed in the vagina arrests conception. It should be administered with rice-water or water boiled with *taṇḍulī* roots.
If the vaginal opening is fumigated with the wood of the *niṃba* tree according to the prescribed method, then at the end of the menstrual period, it prevents the pain of conception.

The mantra for immobilization: *Oṃ garbhaṃ staṃbhaya*. [Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "Immobilization," in the *Śrī Dattātreyatantra*]. Now, regarding the incantation for causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), the Lord said: Listen to the great and wondrous incantation for causing enmity, as taught by the perfected one (*siddha*). Having consecrated a single hand with a crow’s wing and the other hand with an owl’s wing, one should wrap the tip of a *malati* flower with black thread. Then, with water, one should offer libations into the hollow of the joined palms (*añjali*) upon whichever side [of the conflict] one desires. Thus...

One should perform the ritual of *samīdana* and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Taking hair from an elephant, taking a single strand of hair from a lion, and taking earth from the footprints of a cat (*paṭolī*) on the ground, one should place a fire upon that and offer oblations of *mālatī* flowers. This causes enmity for whomever it is directed; it is not otherwise than as declared by Śaṅkara.

Taking the dung of a crow in battle, taking the dung of a rat, and mixing it with earth from the footprints [of an enemy], men should wrap it in blue cloth and, having drunk the mantra, cast it [upon the enemy].

By this [rite] involving a hundred [recitations], enmity arises at that very moment between brothers or father and son. A man should take the hair of a brown snake (*sarpadaṃta*) and, mixing it with funeral ashes (*citābhasma*), form it into a pill. Having consecrated it with mantras while naming the individuals, he should cast it into the ground in a garden; enmity arises at that very moment, for what was spoken by Śaṅkara is never otherwise. Furthermore, when the hair of a brown snake is offered as incense in an assembly, enmity arises between them; what was spoken by Śaṅkara is never otherwise.

Having taken horse-hair and a cat's claw, if incense is offered in the assembly hall, enmity indeed arises. Having taken honey and feces, one should grind them with a snake’s fang; having applied a tilaka-mark on the forehead, enmity arises instantly. Having taken an elephant’s tusk and a lion’s fang, one should grind them with human teeth; by grinding them with butter, it causes enmity.

Taking the hair of a horse and the hair of a buffalo, if incense is offered in the assembly hall, enmity arises instantly. Taking the neck-hair of a lion and burying it far away in the ground, constant quarreling arises and enmity then ensues. Whosoever has enmity toward another, or if one wishes for a living being to live in opposition to another, one should properly fashion an effigy from clay mixed with the dust of the enemy's footprint and bury it in a cremation ground.

[The seventh chapter, named "Subjugation," in that very Tantra. Now, the subjugation of women. On a Saturday, having taken the sandals from a woman, having applied a tilaka on her left breast, and having gathered her hair, one should wrap it in blue cloth.

Having smeared the vulva with vermilion (sindūra) along with semen, one should bury it at the left side of the door. Whoever steps over it comes under one's control, even at the cost of their life or wealth.

This should not be given to just anyone; it is difficult even for the gods to obtain. If a man applies the ashes of the *brahmadaṇḍī* funeral pyre to a woman's body, that woman becomes submissive; it is not otherwise, as declared by Śaṅkara.

Taking a *puṅgī* fruit on a Monday during the *mṛga* nakṣatra, one who places a piece of it infused with its own juice into betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) becomes a subduer of all. Having taken the flesh of a camel (*uṣṭra*), one should give it for her to eat and drink; this yoga is said to succeed even without a mantra. Barley powder, turmeric (*haridrā*), one's own urine, ghee, and mustard seeds, combined with the juice of betel— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

The wise man should not consume it; he whose feet become like water attains a luster like that of a lotus and becomes beloved by all women and in royal households. It must not be given to anyone else; it was spoken by Śaṅkara. This is to be given to each individual alone, for it is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (7) Now, the mantra: *Oṃ namo 'dirūpāya amukam ākarṣaṇaṃ kuru kuru svāhā*. One should recite it one hundred and eight times;

One who recites [the mantra] with a one-pointed mind attains success; this mantra, which begins with *Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ namaḥ*, belongs to the side that destroys inauspiciousness and brings about the destruction of inauspiciousness. One should recite it ten thousand times (*ayuta*). Seated at the root of a *tulasī* plant, one should recite with a one-pointed mind; one will suddenly obtain a kingdom—this was spoken by Śaṅkara, and not otherwise. Seated upon an *aṅkola* tree, one should recite with a one-pointed mind; one becomes a king of kings—this was spoken by Śaṅkara, and not otherwise. The mantra is *Oṃ hyoṃ*.

"Oṃ vāṃ mayi namaḥ"—one should recite this ten thousand times for success. Seated upon an *apāmārga* plant, one should recite it with a one-pointed mind; all undertakings will be accomplished, not otherwise. This was spoken by Śaṅkara. Seated upon an *uḍumbara* tree, one should recite it with a one-pointed mind; mastery over speech (*vācāsiddhi*) will come to pass. This is true; it was spoken by Śaṅkara, not otherwise. The accomplishment of all types [is achieved] through fourteen [recitations]. *Oṃ śrīṃ*, salutation to Śāradā; one should recite this ten thousand times for success. Seated upon a *guñjā* plant in the sky, one should recite with a one-pointed mind; the bird named Saṃtoṣa grants whatever else is desired. *Oṃ*, salutation to the Mother of the World (*Jaganmātṛ*); one should recite this ten thousand times for success at the Great God’s single *liṅga*.

One should always worship Kālī, offering incense and reciting the mantra one thousand times at the three junctions of the day for one month; then Paṇī, the beautiful celestial maiden, will not depart.
